newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open mostly higher amid euphoria. [CORRECTED 16:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open mostly higher amid euphoria. [CORRECTED 16:50 GMT]

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices recovered from weakness in overseas trading to open mostly higher on Wednesday, amid the belief the Federal Reserve will leave rates steady for the forseeable future.

"There are people who have to and want to buy the market," said Mead Briggs, head of proprietary trading at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp. "I don't know anyone other than short-term traders willing to sell."
The 30-year bond was at 102-29/32, up 5/32 from late Tuesday. Its yield fell to 6.40 percent from 6.42 percent.
The bond's yield fell to its lowest level since closing at 6.40 percent on December 4.
With the two-year note's yield at 5.86 percent, the spread between the two-year and 30-year narrowed to a pretty thin 54 basis points. (Corrects from 46 to 54 basis points.)

The euphoria -- mostly at the long end, since the short end cannot move much with the market still expecting a rate hike at some point -- comes on the heels of Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before a House banking subcommittee on Tuesday afternoon.
Greenspan testifies before the Senate Banking Committee on Wednesday at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.

Few players think Greenspan will change his tune from Tuesday, in which he gave an upbeat assessment of the U.S. economy. He noted that economic growth was slowing from its robust pace earlier in the year and suggested that the Fed would not have to raise rates at this time.

But, he cautioned that with "considerable momentum behind the expansion and labor market and market utilization rates unusually high, the Fed must be alert to the possibility that additional action might be called for to forestall excessive credit creation."
Within moments, Treasury yields dropped more than 10 basis points.
Gains were extended in the Tokyo session during the night. Profit-taking in London erased those gains only, but losses were brief as buying took over early in the U.S.
"The mood to buy the dip," said Neil DeSarno, head trader at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp. "Any pullback will be bought."
Yet any attempts at a rally on Wednesday could stall ahead of the Treasury's $11.5 billion five-year note auction, traders said.

In early trading, the when-issued five-year note was at 6.05 percent, well below its 6.18 percent level seen on Monday. Traders said investors would love to get the issue back above 6.10 percent but doubt it would. Some said that after the auction it would not be a surprise to take the issue to 6.00 percent.
"The five-year note, given the bull market, looks cheap, so it should do well after the auction," said DeSarno.
On Tuesday, the Treasury successfully sold $15.5 billion two-year notes at 5.93 percent. The issue has since rallied to 5.85 percent.
The two-year note's price was at 100-1/32, unchanged.
Outstanding five-year notes were unchanged at 100-27/32 to yield 6.05 percent and 10-year notes were up 1/32 to 103-21/32, yielding 6.12 percent.
The three-month, six-month and year-bills were down one basis point each at 5.07 percent, 5.13 percent and 5.23 percent, respectively.
